subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the Edexcel spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE Edexcel Sociology simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: 'Social stratification' means...
options: The division of society into layers or ranks (e.g. by class, status or power)
questions.explain: Stratification is the hierarchical ranking of groups in society into unequal layers.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes 'social class'?
options: A group sharing the same religion
A group sharing a similar economic position (e.g. occupation, income, wealth)
questions.explain: Social class is a way of ranking people by their economic position, such as occupation and income.

questions.q: The key difference between wealth and income is that...
options: Wealth is assets already owned (e.g. property, savings); income is money received regularly (e.g. wages)
questions.explain: Wealth is accumulated assets; income is a flow of money such as wages, salary or benefits.

questions.q: A person's monthly salary is an example of their...
questions.explain: A salary is money received regularly, i.e. income, not accumulated wealth.

questions.q: Karl Marx argued society is divided mainly into two classes based on...
options: Ownership of the means of production (bourgeoisie vs proletariat)
questions.explain: Marx divided society by ownership of the means of production: bourgeoisie (owners) and proletariat (workers).

questions.q: In Marxist theory, the working class accepting their exploitation as normal is called...
questions.explain: False class consciousness is the proletariat's failure to recognise their exploitation.

questions.q: Max Weber argued stratification is based on three dimensions:
questions.explain: Weber identified three linked dimensions: class (economic), status (social honour) and party (power).

questions.q: How does Weber differ from Marx on class?
options: Weber saw more complex divisions and added status and power, not just ownership
Weber said there are no classes
questions.explain: Weber accepted economic class but added status and power, seeing a more complex, multi-layered structure.

questions.q: In Weber's theory, 'status' refers to...
options: The social honour or prestige attached to a person or group
questions.explain: For Weber, status is the level of social honour or prestige a group holds.

questions.q: 'Absolute poverty' is best defined as...
options: Lacking the basic resources needed to survive (e.g. food, shelter, clean water)
Being poorer than most people in your society
questions.explain: Absolute poverty is lacking the minimum resources needed for survival.

questions.q: A family that cannot afford things considered normal in their society (e.g. a holiday, warm home) experiences...
questions.explain: Relative poverty means being unable to afford the living standards considered normal in that society.

questions.q: 'Life chances' are...
options: The opportunities a person has to obtain good things like health, education and housing
questions.explain: Life chances are one's opportunities to achieve valued outcomes such as good health, education and housing.

questions.q: Weber argued that a person's class position strongly affects their...
questions.explain: Weber linked class to differing life chances: better-off groups access better health, housing and education.

questions.q: Weber described 'authority' as...
options: Power seen as legitimate and accepted by those it is exercised over
questions.explain: Authority is legitimate power that people accept, unlike coercion which relies on force.

questions.q: A monarch inheriting the throne is an example of which of Weber's types of authority?
questions.explain: Traditional authority rests on long-established customs, such as an inherited monarchy.

questions.q: 'Social mobility' refers to...
options: Movement of individuals or groups up or down the class structure
Changing jobs within the same class
questions.explain: Social mobility is movement between social positions/classes, upwards or downwards.

questions.q: A person born into a working-class family who becomes a wealthy professional has experienced...
questions.explain: Rising to a higher class position is upward social mobility.

questions.q: In a caste system, a person's position is mainly...
questions.explain: Caste is a closed system where status is ascribed at birth and cannot normally be changed.

questions.q: The 'gender pay gap' is evidence that stratification also occurs by...
questions.explain: The gender pay gap shows women and men are stratified unequally by gender in the labour market.

questions.q: When minority ethnic groups face poorer life chances due to discrimination, this is an example of stratification by...
questions.explain: Ethnic inequality in areas like pay and employment is stratification by ethnicity.
